Hello HN! I am Zigao, a high school student from Shanghai. I am new to HN so hello to y’all!

I used Arc everyday, and I never had any issues with it. So when The Browser Company announced that they will shut down Arc on Dec 22 I was devastated. I don’t want to switch back to boring tabs along the top. Everything else i’ve tried is either a Chromium fork or an AI integrated browser that I don’t want. Therefore, I’ve been building my own browser for the last three weeks. Its name is Zigzag, a free and open source Mac browser that works just like Arc, written in Swift and based on WebKit. It is lightweight and fast.

Zigzag has:

- The stuff you missed from Arc (obviously, that’s the point)...

- Import from Arc (or any other browser) brings everything (your spaces, pins, history, passwords, cookies, etc)

- Chrome extension support! Even though its based on WebKit, you can install them from the Chrome Web Store. Extensions such as 1Password, Bitwarden, dark reader, Return Youtube Dislike, Tampermonkey all work)

And most importantly:

- Privacy: no account, no telemetry, no analytics

- Free and open source: no one can shut it down, anyone can contribute and fork their own copy!

- It’s tiny and fast! Around 18 MB installed (Arc is over 800 MB), no Chromium, no Electron (eww)

Some minor features that are nice-to-haves:

- Built in ad blocker using uBlock origin’s and Easylist’s filter lists

- Cookie popups turned down for you automatically, never accepted

- Split view up to four pages, drag pages intuitively

- Install any website as apps (still polishing it)

- Developer mode for web devs

- Little Arc (called Zigzag Mini)

- AI apps can use your browser if you want (MCP, off by default), stop button built in

- AppleScript and Shortcuts support, written in the conventional way

Why WebKit?

- I once tried to fork Helium and build on that. But the source was around 100 GB and builds took 3 to 4 hours on my Mac. Shipping Chromium is nearly impossible for me as a solo dev

- Battery and RAM: WebKit is built for Mac by Apple, its generally easier on battery and memory than Chromium

- Native: Swift + WebKit = behaves like a real Mac app, explained later (e.g. Zen)

- Chrome extensions already works on Zigzag, so the point of using Chromium is mostly gone

Why not Zen or Orion?

I tried both before building this, because I was looking for alternatives. They are good browsers, just not what I wanted.

Zen is based on Firefox. It is basically an Arc replica but it’s a Firefox under the hood, so you get Firefox extensions instead of Chrome extensions, and it doesn’t really feel like a native Mac app, which was kinda backwards. If you love Firefox it’s great, but it didn’t feel like Arc to me.

Orion is the closest to what I wanted in terms of speed, lightweightness and nativeness (are these even words?). It is WebKit and runs Chrome extensions. But it is closed sourced, and it is nowhere like Arc. It has vertical tabs but no real spaces, pins or favorites like Arc. It feels like a Safari clone instead of an Arc clone, so I turned it down. I love how it supports Chrome extensions, so that’s why I’ve done the same in Zigzag.

So how do Chrome extensions work on WebKit?

This is probably the part people ask about the most, so here you go.

In macOS 15.4, Apple added web extension support to WebKit itself. Safari only takes extensions that come wrapped in an app from the App store, but the engine underneath can load a normal Chrome extension folder. So when you click “Add to Zigzag” on the Chrome Web Store, Zigzag downloads the extension straight from Google. It checks its signatures, unpacks it, and hands it to WebKit.

That’s the easy part, and frankly most WebKit browsers can do that easily. However, WebKit doesn’t have every Chrome API. Stuffy like history, bookmarks, downloads, side panels, notifications and a few others just aren’t there. So Zigzag fills those in itself. When an extension calls one, Zigzag answers it, but only if that extension asked for that permission. 1Password and Bitwarden works, because they talk to their Mac apps the same way they do in Chrome.

The hardest one was Tampermonkey. WebKit has no userScripts API at all, so I had to build my own on top of WebKit’s content scripts, with each extension’s scripts kept separate from the extension itself like in Chrome.

What doesn’t work yet:

- the debugger API (so things that control the browser like Claude for Chrome cant control the pages, but there’s MCP that you can turn on if you want)

- Chrome’s own Google sign in for extensions (chrome.identity)

- Some old way of blocking requests that some extensions still use (webRequest from manifest V2) (e.g. uBlock origin full doesn’t work, but lite version works)

Most popular extensions are fine though. If any extension doesn’t work, leave a comment below or open an issue and I will look into it.

How I build it

Honest up front: I built Zigzag with the help from Claude Code. But it is not another piece of AI slop app. I decide what it does and how it should feel, and every change goes through my own daily browsing before it ships. It is my daily browser now for three weeks, and I am just like any of you, I don’t want trash apps! Claude writes most of the code, but I am the one reviewing the quality, the functions and the UI/UX decisions. Try it out yourself or open a PR if you can do better!

What’s missing

It is still a beta. No sync between Macs yet (passwords sync through iCloud keychain though). No boosts or easels. Needs macOS 15.4 or newer.

Try it

https://zigzagbrowser.com

https://github.com/ZigaoWang/zigzag

If you try it I’d love to know what didn’t went so well (or what did went well!), which extensions you need, and any sites that break. I read every issue on GitHub and every comment below! Thank you for your time!

I know that many folks here post their personal emails in the Who's for Hire monthly pages and other places, and want to remind you that this public site gets views from folks with ill intent (or their bots/agents) as well. I use unique emails for every site, so I immediately knew that the late AWS payments email sent to my HN email were fake. There were other tells, but I want to remind everyone to be vigilant! HN is public but even social media sites where you supposedly can make your page private I've had some of those emails suddenly have spam sent to as well. Please be safe everyone!

My favorite tells that an email is a scam: - Before opening a surprising/suspicious email, hover over the sender name to see the domain the sender came from (don't open the email if it's strange). - _If_ you already opened the email, before clicking any links in the email, hover over them to see the domain that the link sends you to.

There are dozens more tips but a full article would be required, and these two will prevent you from falling for nearly all of them.

Hi HN, I'm James, one of the co-founders of Coral.

Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs that they can save as custom tools to reuse.

You can publish custom tools for groups of agents, so your team’s library of tools adapts to your unique systems, data and use cases. Custom tools help agent performance and give more precise units of permission control.

Here’s a short demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0PKOlHLyVI

We started on this while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry data and undocumented relationships across internal and external systems. It took broad permissions, a lot of tokens and it would start from scratch the next time.

We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent writes the steps that worked into a program and saves it as a custom tool. Next time, the agent finds that custom tool in the same search as standard provider tools (e.g. Datadog, Slack), and reuses it. It started with SRE, but we (and our early users) now use Coral for agent work across the org.

For our tasks across GitHub, Linear and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools help agents work 29% faster, at 31% lower cost (tasks here: https://withcoral.com/docs/examples/custom-tools).

Coral builds on code mode, adding custom tools, policy controls and managed identities. Each program runs in a V8 isolate with no network access or credentials. Coral checks every tool call against workspace policy before attaching credentials and forwarding it to the provider. You can configure each provider to use the caller’s own account, so teammates can share tools without sharing API tokens. (e.g. https://withcoral.com/blog/slackbot-works-better-with-coral)

Coral is written in Rust, and you can run it as a desktop app or as a shared server. The core is Apache 2.0 and has no limits on users, agents or volume. Everything I've described here is in the OSS edition. SAML, SCIM, and org-wide governance features will be available soon under an enterprise licence.

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. You can download it here https://withcoral.com/download.

I'll be in the comments here and on Slack: https://withcoral.com/slack

Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots.

Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA

We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.

The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.

When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.

We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.

Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.

Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.

So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.

If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!

Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :)

What it does today:

- Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router.

- Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks.

- Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance.

We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results.

But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now.

We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions:

- 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency)

-The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps.

Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels.

So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8.

The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within

There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections.

You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:

https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...

Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback.

Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai.

We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.

Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.

Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.

I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.

We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.

Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence

We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)

Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.

We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).

We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.

To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.

Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.

We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!
